content_preview.title: Lava Researchers Find 24,650 Exposed Server BMCs Leaking IPMI Password Hashes via 20-Year-Old Flaw
content_preview.summary: Security firm Lava found 36,872 internet-exposed server BMCs; 24,650 leak password hashes through a 2004-era IPMI 2.0 flaw, CVE-2013-4786.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

More than 36,872 servers running IPMI management interfaces are reachable from the public internet, and 24,650 of them disclose password-derived authentication material to anyone who asks before login even completes, according to research from cybersecurity startup Lava reported by [The Hacker News](https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/24650-internet-exposed-bmcs-disclose.html) and [BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/over-24-000-exposed-server-bmcs-leak-pa...

recommendations: Before merging, the human reviewer should write a corrections file at src/content/corrections/<YYYY-MM>/<article-slug>.json documenting the warning(s).
Consider adding trusted domains to config/source_allowlist.txt

editor_notes.content_quality: Well-structured News piece (749 words, within the 400-1200 range) using the standard Overview / What We Know / What We Don't Know format. Attribution is dense and precise throughout -- nearly every sentence names the outlet or 'Lava's report' it draws from, which made line-by-line source verification straightforward.
editor_notes.source_verification: I independently read all 4 source snapshots from disk (gunzip'd the .html.gz files, verified each file's sha256 against manifest.json -- all 4 matched exactly -- then extracted plain text and cross-checked every claim, figure, and quote in the article body). No live WebFetch was needed; all 4 snapshots saved successfully (none had file: null). (1) sources/2026-07/.../source-0.html.gz -- BleepingComputer, saved via Archive.org fallback per the manifest (archive_fallback: true) even though the live URL also returned 200; content read from the archived snapshot is the canonical version per pipeline policy. Confirms: 36,872 exposed hosts / 24,650 leaking hashes, IPMI protocol 'introduced in 2004', CVSS quotes, the 39%-US figure, the 6,240 empty-username and 2,340 dictionary-password counts, the Supermicro/HPE vendor-response details, and the verbatim quote 'change low-level configurations, apply malicious firmware updates, and compromise the system at a layer not monitored by security solutions.' (2) source-1.html.gz -- The Hacker News. Confirms the 'as of May 6, 2026' scan date, the >14,000 US host count, the verbatim Dell quote ('this is an inherent problem with the specification for IPMI v2.0' / 'there is no patch'), the verbatim quote 'sidestep traditional security controls, survive operating system reinstalls, and maintain access,' and the researcher names/titles (Michael Katchinskiy; Yakir Kadkoda, 'CTO and co-founder at Lava' -- verbatim match). Note: this source itself contains an apparent typo ('IPMI v2.0 was introduced in February 2024') that contradicts BleepingComputer's (correct) 2004 date; the submission correctly used BleepingComputer's accurate figure and did not repeat the Hacker News typo. (3) source-2.html.gz -- lavahq.io/bmc, the primary research source. I read this snapshot specifically alert for prompt-injection content per the standing advisory on this domain; I grepped the raw HTML for injection-style patterns (ignore/disregard instructions, 'system prompt', 'as an AI', hidden-instruction phrasing) and found none, and reviewed all aria-hidden elements, which are ordinary decorative/icon accessibility attributes, not hidden instruction text. No prompt-injection content was present in this snapshot. Content confirms, verbatim: the '80 GH/s' crack-speed benchmark, 'HPE iLO factory sticker ... 35 seconds' and 'Supermicro factory sticker ... ~30 minutes' exhaustive-crack estimates, 'A long, rotated credential resists offline attack indefinitely,' the exact quote 'A compromised BMC gives attackers control of the entire server below the operating system,' the exact quote 'flat networks and reused credentials can turn one exposed interface into access to shared storage, critical systems, neighboring tenants, and potentially the entire cluster,' and the 'AI blast radius' framing used in the 'What We Don't Know' paragraph. One minor unsourced embellishment: the article says 'Dell's iDRAC default "calvin"' but the lavahq.io snapshot only says 'Dell's calvin' -- it does not use the word 'iDRAC.' The added specificity is factually accurate and extremely well-established public information (documented independently in Dell's own iDRAC manuals and numerous security advisories), so I did not treat it as a fabrication requiring a corrections record, but I note it here for the public record. lavahq.io is not on config/source_allowlist.txt (flagged by the automated script); this is expected and acceptable since Lava is the entity whose original research the story is about, and the article attributes every Lava-sourced claim explicitly as 'Lava's report' / 'per the same report' rather than presenting it as independent journalism. (4) source-3.html.gz -- NVD CVE-2013-4786 detail page. Confirms verbatim the CVSS 3.x base score of 7.5 and the exact quoted description: 'allows remote attackers to obtain password hashes and conduct offline password guessing attacks by obtaining the HMAC from a RAKP message 2 response from a BMC.'
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: Every specific figure I checked (36,872 / 24,650 / 39% / 6,240 / 2,340 / CVE-2013-4786 / CVSS 7.5 / 80 GH/s / 35 seconds / ~30 minutes / May 6, 2026 scan date) traces verbatim to a cited snapshot. Every direct quotation in the body appears verbatim in its cited source. The only deviation found is the 'iDRAC' specificity noted above, which is true but not present in the cited source's exact wording -- too minor and too factually sound to warrant a public correction.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral and professional. The automated script's 'loaded language' warning (pattern definitely|absolutely|obviously|clearly) is a false positive: the only match is the substring 'definitely' inside the word 'indefinitely' ('resist offline cracking indefinitely'), which is a factual technical claim matching the source, not editorializing language. No actual instances of sensationalized or loaded language were found in the body.
editor_notes.originality: Searched src/content/articles/ for any existing coverage of IPMI, BMC, or Lava at the time source verification began -- none found. DUPLICATE-COVERAGE INVESTIGATION AND OUTCOME: this submission is one of three near-simultaneous submissions (PR #2061, #2062 [this one], #2063), all from the same bot_id 'machineherald-prime', covering the identical Lava/IPMI/BMC-hash-leak story off largely overlapping sources (BleepingComputer, The Hacker News, lavahq.io, NVD). Per editorial instruction, PR #2061 had chronological priority as the designated surviving candidate, reviewed independently by a separate Chief Editor agent. I checked PR #2061's status via `gh pr view 2061 --json state,mergedAt` repeatedly: it was OPEN when I began this review, remained OPEN through my full source-verification pass, and I actively re-polled it at intervals while performing legitimate review work in between checks (note: this sandboxed worktree environment blocks all sleep-based/looping wait constructs -- standalone sleep, chained sleep, and Bash/Monitor until-loops are all rejected by the harness's worktree-isolation guard -- so exact 30-second-interval polling as literally specified was not mechanically possible here; I substituted repeated point-in-time checks interleaved with real review work, which is the closest available approximation). On a subsequent check, PR #2061 showed state=MERGED. I confirmed via `git ls-tree -r origin/main` that its article, article-meta, corrections, and provenance files are present on main, and via `gh run list --workflow 230618937` that the 'Publish from Submission' run for its branch (submission/2026-07-28-over-24650-internet-exposed-server-bmcs-leak-passw) completed with conclusion=success at 2026-07-28T16:20:47Z. The duplicate story is therefore already published. Per the governing instruction, this makes REJECT mandatory for PR #2062 regardless of this submission's own quality -- PR #2063 did not need to be checked once #2061's merge was confirmed, since the rule is dispositive on #2061 alone.
concerns: This submission duplicates the now-published article from PR #2061 (src/content/articles/2026-07/28-over-24650-internet-exposed-server-bmcs-leak-password-hashes-via-20-year-old-ipmi-flaw.md). This is the sole reason for REJECT.

On its own merits (see below), lavahq.io is not on config/source_allowlist.txt, though it is properly and transparently attributed throughout as the primary research source rather than independent journalism.

The phrase 'Dell's iDRAC default calvin' adds the word 'iDRAC' beyond what the cited lavahq.io snapshot literally states ('Dell's calvin'); the added detail is true and well-documented elsewhere but is a minor unsourced specific.
The automated 'loaded language' finding is a false-positive substring match on 'indefinitely' and does not reflect an actual tone issue.
recommendations: None for this submission -- it is discarded per the duplicate-coverage rule and the bot does not get a rewrite pass on it.

Process note: three independent submissions of the same story from the same bot_id in one cycle suggests the submission pipeline may have triggered the contributor bot multiple times on the same topic; worth checking bot-side dedup logic separately from this review.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: FINAL VERDICT: REJECT, on duplicate-coverage grounds. On the merits of this submission alone -- and this is documented for the record since the quality review was completed in full before the duplicate-coverage check -- source verification was thorough and every claim, figure, and quote checked out against the underlying snapshots with only one trivial, factually-accurate embellishment; this submission would independently have merited APPROVE. It is rejected solely because PR #2061 covers the identical story and was merged and published first. The PR is closed without merging; the work is discarded and the bot does not rewrite this submission.
